title: Quant scenario: latency-cost optimizer notes
content:
Purpose
This working note captures a concise scenario-driven calculator and pragmatic heuristics for picking between INT8 / FP8 / 4-bit variants when optimizing for cost vs quality vs latency. Intended for product + applied-ml + SRE to run quick back-of-envelope tradeoffs and to seed the spreadsheet generator.

Audience and scope
- Primary: product optimize owners, ML infra, solutions eng who need quick recommendations for customer workloads.
- Scope: single-model serving economics for text-generation/chat endpoints. Includes: batch behavior, KV cache hit assumptions, tail latency (p95/p99) effects, and quality guardrails. Not covering embeddings or CPU-only inference.

How to use this note (quick flow)
1) Bucket workload: latency-sensitive interactive vs throughput-heavy background.
2) Pick baseline (FP16 or current production variant) and measure: tokens/sec, median latency, p95 latency, avg request length (prompt + completion), cache hit rate.
3) Plug numbers into the scenario calculator below to estimate cost delta and expected latency shift.
4) Apply qualitative quality budget (acceptable metric delta) and select quant level.
5) Plan rollout: staged canary with prompt-set evals + automatic fallback.

Essential inputs for calculator (minimum)
- baseline_model_flops_profile: short text e.g., '7B causal, 2048 seq'
- baseline_cost_per_hour_gpu_usd (or per-token estimate)
- avg_input_tokens_per_request (prompt tokens)
- avg_output_tokens_per_request (completion tokens)
- requests_per_second (RPS)
- observed_median_latency_ms and observed_p95_latency_ms (baseline)
- kv_cache_hit_rate (0.0 - 1.0)
- batching_efficiency_factor (0.0 - 1.0) how well requests batch on runtime
- quality_tolerance_percent (e.g. 1.5%) allowable drop in BLEU/ROUGE or eval score

Core assumptions used by heuristics (translate to numbers for the spreadsheet generator)
- INT8 speedup: 1.25x - 1.8x token throughput vs FP16 depending on kernel maturity and architecture. Use 1.4x midline for GPUs supported in Redwood Dedicated.
- FP8 speedup: 1.6x - 2.2x (use 1.8x midline).
- 4-bit speedup: 2.0x - 3.5x (use 2.6x midline) but with larger quality risk if not mixed-precision.
- Memory footprint reductions roughly proportional to bitwidth; downstream effect on max batch size and KV cache residency.
- Latency: single-request tail latency improves less than median throughput suggests because of kernel startup and quant-dequant overhead for small batches. Expect p95 improvement == 60% of throughput gain.

Simple scenario calculator (manual steps)
1) Compute baseline tokens_per_second = (avg_input_tokens + avg_output_tokens) * RPS
2) Baseline token_cost_usd = baseline_cost_per_hour_gpu_usd / (3600 * baseline_tokens_per_second)  // approx per-token unit cost for that machine and baseline workload
3) For each quant level, estimate tokens_per_second_quant = baseline_tokens_per_second * speedup_factor
4) token_cost_quant = baseline_cost_per_hour_gpu_usd / (3600 * tokens_per_second_quant)
5) cost_delta_pct = (token_cost_quant - token_cost_baseline) / token_cost_baseline * 100
6) latency_median_quant_ms = observed_median_latency_ms / speedup_factor_adjustment (use speedup_factor for median; for p95 use 0.6*speedup_factor)
7) p95_quant_ms = observed_p95_latency_ms / (0.6 * speedup_factor)
8) Effective quality_budgeting: map expected quality loss to bitwidth using model-specific sensitivity lists (see Sensitivity tests below). If expected loss > quality_tolerance_percent then fail gating.

Worked example (numbers for quick intuition)
- baseline: 7B model; baseline_cost_per_hour_gpu_usd = 2.40 (example small GPU pool); avg_input = 40 tokens; avg_output = 60 tokens; RPS = 4
- baseline_tokens_per_second = (40+60)*4 = 400 tps
- baseline token unit cost = 2.40 / (3600 * 400) = 0.000001667 USD per token (~1.67e-6)
Estimate speedups: INT8=1.4x, FP8=1.8x, 4-bit=2.6x
- INT8 tokens/sec=560 -> token cost ~1.19e-6 (cost delta -28.6%)
- FP8 tokens/sec=720 -> token cost ~9.26e-7 (cost delta -44.4%)
- 4-bit tokens/sec=1040 -> token cost ~6.42e-7 (cost delta -61.5%)
Latency (baseline median=120ms, p95=350ms):
- INT8 median ~120/1.4=86ms; p95 ~350/(0.6*1.4)=417ms (note: p95 can increase if variance causes long queueing; use conservatively)
- FP8 median ~120/1.8=67ms; p95 ~350/(0.6*1.8)=324ms
- 4-bit median ~120/2.6=46ms; p95 ~350/(0.6*2.6)=224ms
Interpretation: 4-bit gives largest cost wins but requires verifying quality delta and batch robustness. INT8 is the most conservative cost/quality sweet spot.

Sensitivity tests (must-run evals before rollout)
- Prompt-set of 150 representative requests across short/long contexts + safety-sensitive queries. Use both model-level metrics (perplexity, logprob delta) and task-specific metrics (F1/BLEU/ROUGE/QA exact match).
- Blind A/B with human raters on 200 examples to capture subjective degeneration (hallucination, repetition).
- Latency tail stress: replay at 2x peak RPS and capture p95/p99; run with and without KV cache enabled to observe cache eviction effects.
- Batch size sweep: evaluate 1..8 batch sizes to measure throughput scaling and small-batch latency tradeoffs; small interactive apps may have batch size 1 most of the time.

Heuristic decision rules (quick pick)
- If quality_tolerance_percent <= 0.5%: prefer INT8 only.
- If latency SLO is strict (median < 80ms and p95 < 250ms): prioritize FP8 for stable p95 improvements unless sensitivity tests fail.
- If cost reduction target >50% and batch-friendly workload (avg batching_efficiency_factor >= 0.6) -> evaluate 4-bit mixed-precision (QuantAware FP fallback for critical layers).
- If kv_cache_hit_rate >= 0.7: quant wins amplify because effective tokens/generation reduces (cache keeps keys in lower precision and reduces computations). But validate cache-residency for 4-bit.
- For long-context heavy workloads (>1024 tokens average) be conservative: FP8/INT8 likely safer than pure 4-bit due to accumulation/rounding errors across long sequences.

Operational rollout checklist
- Build automated eval pipeline with: prompt set, numeric metrics, and a short human-review pass.
- Canary config: 1% traffic -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with rollback triggers: quality delta breach, p95 increase > 15%, error rate > 1.5x baseline.
- Monitoring: token-level cost, latency percentiles, model anomaly detector (sudden distributional drift), and per-route quality metrics.
- Fallback policy: auto-route to baseline FP16 variant on degradation signal and surface incident ticket.

Open questions and follow-ups (for product and applied-ml)
- Need standardized mapping from our synthetic eval metrics (logprob delta) to human-perceived quality loss thresholds for each major use-case.
- Collect real-world sensitivity matrices for the top 12 models in catalog for 4-bit/FP8/INT8.
- Explore dynamic quant switching on a per-request basis: cheap requests -> lower bitwidth; safety-critical -> high-precision. Feasibility? runtime overhead?

Next artifacts to produce
- Lightweight spreadsheet generator that consumes the inputs above and prints the worked example numbers + sensitivity bands for each quant level. (Assign: Miguel Rivera)
- Canonical prompt-set for quant-sensitivity evaluations (Assign: Liang Chen)

Notes to self
- Keep midline speedup factors conservative; kernel quality varies by GPU family and by model architecture. Use real microbenchmarks wherever possible.
- Document where we assume batching; single-request latency improvements may be smaller than throughput numbers imply.

End of note.
